chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from one of his companions, from Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari, who said:

I entered upon Abu al-Hasan, the Master of the Camp (peace be upon him), and a boy from his children came and handed him a rose. He kissed it and placed it on his eyes, then handed it to me and said: 'O Abu Hashim! Whoever takes a rose or a basil leaf, kisses it, and places it on his eyes, then sends blessings upon Muhammad and the Family of Muhammad, the Imams, Allah will write for him good deeds equal to the sand of 'Araj, and erase from him bad deeds equal to that.'

key_terms.صَاحِبِ الْعَسْكَرِ: Master of the Camp (title for Imam al-Hasan al-Askari)
key_terms.عَالِجٍ: A region known for its vast sand, used as a measure of abundance

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for kissing a rose or basil and sending blessings upon the Imams?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Askari (peace be upon him) illustrates the spiritual merit of venerating fragrant plants, specifically basil and roses, by kissing them and placing them on the eyes before sending blessings upon the Prophet and the Imams. This practice, rooted in Shia tradition as a form of *taqarrub* (seeking closeness to God) through appreciation of creation, is promised to yield good deeds equal to the sand of 'Araj and erase an equivalent amount of sins. The emphasis on 'Araj' highlights the immense scale of reward, connecting physical acts of reverence with profound spiritual purification.
